planting.note: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight.

directions: Sow seed around or just after last frost at the foot of a tall, sturdy trellis, since this runner-type bean is a vigorous climber that needs a strong structure to support its weight through the season. Grown for centuries in the volcanic soils around La Granja de San Ildefonso in Segovia, Spain, it produces some of the largest bean seeds in cultivation — broad, flat, and ivory-white — traditionally simmered slowly into the region's celebrated judión stew. Like other runner beans it flowers and sets pods best where summer nights stay relatively cool, dropping blossoms in prolonged heat. Leave pods on the vine until fully dry and papery before shelling the outsized beans for storage.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
European Commission Protected Geographical Indication registry

planting.note: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support.

directions: Direct sow around last frost at the base of a tall trellis or pole tepee, as this Mesoamerican runner bean climbs vigorously and rewards a sturdy support with a long season of striking scarlet-purple flowers that draw hummingbirds. Ayocote beans have been cultivated in the highlands of central and southern Mexico since long before European contact, and the deep purple-black seeds of this particular landrace are prized in Oaxacan and other regional cuisines for their dense, meaty texture and earthy flavor once cooked. Like other runner beans, it sets pods best when nights stay cool, so growers in hot-summer regions may see reduced yields in high summer. Allow pods to dry completely on the vine before shelling for the best storage-quality dry bean.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination.

directions: Direct sow once the soil has warmed well after last frost, since this bush-type dry bean, like most common beans, resents cold or waterlogged ground at germination. Also sold as Mayocoba or canary bean, Peruano is a pale golden-yellow bean central to everyday Mexican and Mexican-American cooking, valued for a creamy texture and mild flavor that holds up well in refried preparations. The compact bush habit needs no staking and produces a concentrated harvest suited to home drying. Let pods mature fully and dry on the plant before shelling, then store the beans in a cool, dry, airtight container.
sources: University of California, Davis Dry Bean Breeding Program

planting.note: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in.

directions: Direct sow in early spring a few weeks ahead of the last frost, since young lentil plants tolerate light frost and grow best through a long, cool stretch before summer heat sets in. This variety takes its name from the volcanic plateau around Le Puy-en-Velay in France's Auvergne region, where a legally protected growing area produces small, marbled slate-green lentils famous for holding their shape and delivering a peppery, mineral flavor after cooking. Skip heavy nitrogen fertilizer, which pushes leafy growth at the expense of pods, and let the sparse, wiry plants lean on light twiggy brush if needed. Harvest the whole plant once most pods have turned tan and papery, then dry and thresh before storing the seed.
sources: Slow Food Foundation for Biodiversity — Ark of Taste
Institut National de l'Origine et de la Qualité (INAO)

planting.note: Sow directly in cool spring soil a few weeks before last frost, taking advantage of this lentil's tolerance for light frost and cool growing conditions.

directions: Sow directly in cool spring soil a few weeks before last frost, taking advantage of this lentil's tolerance for light frost and cool growing conditions. Black Beluga produces small, glossy, jet-black lentils that resemble caviar once cooked, a resemblance that has made it a favorite of chefs and market growers looking to diversify beyond the common brown lentil. The low, wiry plants need minimal input and thrive in lean soil, since excess fertility encourages foliage over pod set. Harvest the whole plant once the majority of pods have dried and rattle, then thresh and clean before storing the seed in a cool, dry place.
sources: University of Saskatchewan Crop Development Centre

planting.note: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet.

directions: Direct sow after the danger of frost has passed and set a trellis or poles at planting time, since this vigorous Italian climbing bean quickly reaches six to eight feet. Long grown in Italian kitchen gardens, Trionfo Violetto is prized for its double ornamental value — deep violet flowers followed by glossy purple pods — as much as for the table, and the pods turn a deep green when cooked, losing their color but keeping excellent flavor and tenderness. Pick pods young and often, around five to six inches, to encourage continued production and to catch them before they toughen. The striking purple pods also make the plants easy to spot for harvest against their green foliage.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom.

directions: Direct sow after last frost when the soil has warmed, providing poles or a strong trellis for this vigorous climbing heirloom. Nickajack traces its name to a historic Cherokee community in the Tennessee River valley of the southern Appalachians, and it has been passed down among mountain gardeners as a reliable dual-purpose bean, with large, flat pods that can be picked young for snapping or left to mature into tan, speckled dry beans. Harvest at the snap stage for the tenderest eating, around 70 days, or let pods dry fully on the vine for a longer-season soup bean. The vines are productive and well adapted to the humid summers of the Southern Appalachians.
